parties.respondent: The State) Crl. Rev. No.67153 of 2022 (Majid Ali. versus Qamar Abbas, etc.)

holding: So far as Criminal Revision No. 67153 of 2022 filed by the complainant for enhancement of the sentence of the appellant/respondent No.1, Qamar Abbas, awarded by the trial court, is concerned, for the reasons aforesaid, the same is devoid of any legal force, which is accordingly dismissed.

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 14.10.2026. Appellant by: Mr. Ali Hussain, Advocate. State by: Ms. Maida Sobia, Deputy Prosecutor General with Nadeem A.S.I. Complainant by: M/s Muhammad Irfan Malik and Muhammad Barjees Tahir, Advocates with complainant. -------------- AALIA NEELUM, C.J: Qamar Abbas, son of Muhammad Asghar, Gujjar by caste, resident of Jand Sharif, Tehsil Kharian, District Gujrat (hereinafter referred to as “the appellant”), was tried by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Gujrat, in the case arising out of F.I.R. No.244 of 2019, dated 23.12.2019, registered under Sections 302 and 34 PPC at Police Station Gulyana, District Gujrat. Vide judgment dated 06.08.2022, the trial court convicted the appellant under Section 302(b) PPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. He was further directed to pay compensation of Rs.2,00,000/- under Section 544-A Cr.P.C. to the legal heirs of the deceased, Khushnood Akhtar, and, in default of payment thereof, to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months. The benefit of Section 382-B Cr.P.C. was also extended to the appellant.

Aggrieved by the judgment of the trial court, Qamar Abbas (the appellant) has preferred Crl. Appeal No. 67154-J of 2022, challenging his conviction. The complainant has also filed Crl. Rev. No. 67153 of 2022, seeking enhancement of the sentence awarded to the appellant. Since both matters arise out of the same judgment, they are being disposed of through this consolidated judgment.

The prosecution case, as set out in the F.I.R. (Ex. PA), registered on the basis of the written complaint (Ex. PA/1) submitted by Majid Ali, complainant (PW-11), is that on 22.12.2019, at about 08:45 p.m., the complainant, along with Khurram Javed and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), was present at the house of their maternal uncle, Khushnood Akhtar. On hearing a commotion in the street, they rushed outside and saw accused Qamar Abbas, armed with a 12-bore pump-action gun, and two unidentified accused, armed with 30-bore pistols, quarrelling with Khushnood Akhtar. The street was illuminated by electric bulbs. One of the unidentified accused, armed with a 30-bore pistol, approached them and threatened to kill them if any of them would come near him. Accused Qamar Abbas fired successive shots from his 12-bore pump-action gun at Khushnood Akhtar, striking him in the legs. An unidentified accused also fired shots from his pistol at Khushnood Akhtar, hitting him in the legs, whereupon he fell to the ground. Thereafter, all the accused fled northwards on a motorcycle while continuing to fire. The shots fired by the accused also hit Khushnood Akhtar’s white Toyota car bearing registration No.999. The complainant (PW-11), along with Khurram Javed and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), took the injured Khushnood Akhtar to the hospital, but he succumbed to his injuries. Hence, the present case. The motive behind the occurrence was dispute of land.

The initial investigation of the case was conducted by Muhammad Mansha, S.I. (PW-14), who, having found accused Qamar Abbas guilty during the investigation, prepared a challan under section 173, Cr.P.C., and submitted it to the court of competent jurisdiction. Thereafter, the investigation, insofar as it related to accused Arsalan, was entrusted to Yasin Baig, S.I. (PW-13), who likewise found the said accused guilty, prepared a challan under section 173, Cr.P.C., and submitted it to the court of competent jurisdiction. On 20.03.2020, the trial court formally framed a charge against the appellant, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In support of its case, the prosecution examined fourteen (14) witnesses.

Upon conclusion of the prosecution evidence, the statement of the appellant was recorded under Section 342, Cr.P.C. He did not opt to testify on oath in his own defence under Section 340(2), Cr.P.C.; however, he produced documentary evidence comprising a certificate issued by the M.S., THQ Kharian (Mark-DA); a photocopy of the CDR pertaining to mobile phone No. 0300- 8511540 (Mark-DB/1-39); a photocopy of the Nikah Nama dated 23.12.2019 recording the marriage of Suleman Ata of Jand Sharif with Zoya Ahmed (Mark- DC); and a photocopy of the computerized marriage certificate of the said Suleman Ata (Mark-DD). The appellant also examined Faheem Shehzad, Constable (DW-1), through whom he produced the letter dated 08.07.2022 addressed by the DPO, Gujrat, to the RPO, Gujranwala (Ex.DB), along with letter No. 192 dated 07.07.2022 (Ex. DC) and the data pertaining to mobile phone No. 0300-8511540 (Ex.DD). In response to the question as to why the case had been instituted against him and why the prosecution witnesses had deposed against him, the appellant stated as follows: “The complainant of this case is a known property dealer. On the night of 22-12-2019 at 08:00 p.m., according to (weather/p[k/jand-sharif/32.82,73.98) weather history, humidity was 93% and weather condition was fog. At 11:00 pm, humidity increased to 100% weather condition was fog which remained till 11:00 am on 23.12.2019. The occurrence had taken place at dark hours of night and as it was fog, nothing was visible. It is talk of the town that occurrence had taken place at the hands of some dacoits. On the same night i.e. 22/23-12-2019, there was Rasm-e-Hina of one Suleman s/o Ata Ullah r/o village Jand Sharif whose house is quite near to the place of occurrence. After seen the dacoits in the street, the deceased asked the reason for their presence being armed, then as altercation took place between deceased and dacoits which lead to firing. Deceased succumbed to the injuries at the spot but the reports of firing could not be noticed by any person of Jand Sharif due to noise of fire crackers, beating of drums, playing of music on high volume. The presence of deceased was noticed at a later stage. Afterwards a false story of cooked with consultation. The deceased had been spoken by the prosecution having taken him to the hospital for treatment but the record of any hospital does not support this version even the delayed information to the police also speaks volumes of this blind murder. We are two brothers. My elder brother namely Ghulam Abbas had died in year 2014 leaving behind one widow and four kids. My brother owned a plot on a path. The complainant wanted to purchase that plot belonging to the orphans on throw away price. When I noticed this fact, I forbade my widow Bhabi from the sale of that plot. So I earned the displeasure of the complainant who had threatened me of dire consequences. I have been involved in this case by the complainant through false, fabricated story. According to the FIR, the complainant is having cell phone No. 0300-8511540. According to CDR of said phone of complainant collected by police which was afterward taken of from the file, the complainant was present at the time of occurrence at Gulyana and then he proceeded to Margzar Colony, Gujrat City and at later hours of receiving the information of this incident, he posed himself as complainant and eye witness of this case. I produce computerized copy of Pakistan Weather History (weather/pk/jand- sharif/32.82,73.98) Ex-DA (consisting of two pages) dated 22.12.2019 and dated 23.12.2019 Ex-DB (both under objection). I also produce certificate issued by MS THQ Kharian Mark-DA. I also produce photocopy of CDR of phone number 0300-8511540 Mark-DB/1-39. I also produce photocopies of Nikah Nama dated 23.12.2019 of Suleman Ata of Jand Sharif with Zoya Ahmed Mark-DC, photocopy of computerized marriage certificate of said Suleman Ata Mark-DD.”

After recording and appraising the evidence on record in light of the arguments advanced by both sides, the trial court held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and, accordingly, convicted the appellant in the terms stated above.
I have heard the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the parties and have minutely perused the record on the file.

In the instant case, the occurrence took place on 22.12.2019 at 8:45 p.m. at Jand Sharif, falling within the territorial jurisdiction of Police Station Guliana, District Gujrat. According to the prosecution, the appellant, Qamar Abbas, armed with a 12-bore pump-action gun and accompanied by an unidentified person armed with a 30-bore pistol, committed the murder of Khushnood Akhtar (deceased). The place of occurrence was situated at one kilometre from the police station. Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, reported the occurrence to the police at 2:45 a.m. on 23.12.2019 by submitting a written application (Exh-PA/1) to Iftikhar Hussain, ASI (PW-1). Based on the said application, Iftikhar Hussain, ASI (PW-1), registered the FIR (Exh-PA) and thereafter affixed his signatures thereto. The FIR was subsequently forwarded to Muhammad Mansha, SI/SHO (PW-14), for investigation through Nabeel Ashiq 3266/C, who was not cited as a prosecution witness. According to Majid Ali (PW- 11), he, along with Mudasir Iqbal (PW-12) and Khurram Javed (given-up PW), was present at the house of their maternal uncle, Khushnood Akhtar (deceased), when they suddenly heard a noise emanating from the street. All three rushed outside and witnessed the appellant, Qamar Abbas, and two unidentified persons quarrelling and scuffling with the deceased. The streetlights were illuminated at the time. One of the unidentified persons pointed a 30-bore pistol at the witnesses and threatened to kill them if they approached any closer. In their presence, the appellant fired successive shots from his 12-bore pump-action gun at the deceased, striking him in the legs. Thereafter, the unidentified person armed with the 30-bore pistol also fired shots at the deceased, which likewise struck him in the legs. Having sustained serious injuries, the deceased fell to the ground. The accused persons then fled northwards on a motorcycle while resorting to aerial firing. The shots fired by the accused also struck the deceased’s vehicle, a white Toyota Corolla bearing registration No.999 (P-14). Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed that he along with others, shifted Khushnood Akhtar then injured to the hospital in a critically injured condition; however, he succumbed to his injuries. Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, thereafter, reported the occurrence to the police. It is relevant to mention here that Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, did not specify in his written application the time at which the deceased breathed his last. The police proceedings recorded at the foot/bottom of the written application (Exh-PA/1) reflect that the occurrence was reported at 2:45 a.m. on 23.12.2019, whereupon the formal FIR (Exh-PA) was registered. Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, took six hours in reporting the incident for which no explanation is given by him. Furthermore, the complainant offered no explanation for the delay in lodging the report, either in the complaint or in his statement before the trial court. In these circumstances, the possibility of consultation and deliberation on his part prior to lodging the report cannot be ruled out. This constitutes the first infirmity in the prosecution case.

Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, admitted during cross- examination that he had not mentioned in his written application (Exh-PA) the name of the hospital to which Khushnood Akhtar (deceased) had been taken for treatment. He further stated that they reached the hospital approximately 45 minutes after the occurrence and that, five minutes after their arrival, the doctor confirmed the death of the deceased. Dr. Shehroze Amjad (PW-8), however, stated during cross-examination that the interval between the infliction of injuries and death was 30 minutes. The same interval is recorded in the postmortem report (Exh-PF). Thus, according to the medical evidence, the deceased remained alive for approximately 30 minutes after sustaining the injuries, whereas, according to the complainant, they reached the hospital approximately 45 minutes after the occurrence. In view of this discrepancy between the medical evidence and the complainant’s testimony regarding the relevant timeline, it was incumbent upon the prosecution to prove when and where the deceased had breathed his last. In this regard, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed during cross- examination as follows: “It is correct that in application Ex.PA I did not mentioned the name of hospital where the deceased was admitted. Deceased reached hospital after about 45 minutes of the occurrence. There are two private hospitals in Gulyana besides RHC. Village Malika is about one kilometer from place of occurrence. Village Malika and Jand Sharif fall on the same road. There is Govt. hospital at village Malika. I have not produced the death certificate of deceased issued by any hospital. I did not obtain copy of admission register of THQ Khairan. Deceased was pronounced dead after five minutes of reaching emergency ward of hospital. I do no know that FIR was lodged at about 2:45 am on 23.12.2019.” Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), the eyewitness, deposed that the injured had been shifted to the hospital in our car. However, he could not specify the distance between the place of occurrence and the hospital. He further admitted that he did not produce any hospital certificate for substantiating the arrival of the injured for the first time. Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), the eyewitness, deposed during cross-examination as follows: “There is Govt. hospital at Gulyana. --- There is only one hospital in Gulyana which was on road from Gulyana to Dhal Gujran. Distance between Gulyana Chowk and police station is about 01-km. --- I did not produce any hospital certificate regarding victim arrival in the hospital for the first time.” Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), both eyewitnesses of the occurrence, admitted during cross-examination that their respective residences were situated at a considerable distance from the place of occurrence. Majid Ali (PW-11) deposed during cross-examination that: “It is correct that I did not mention the reason of my presence in house of victim at the night of occurrence in FIR”. Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, admitted during cross-examination that his house was approximately three kilometres away from the place of occurrence. Similarly, Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) deposed during cross-examination that: “Village Guliana is about 3 km from our village”. Both witnesses further admitted that they had not disclosed to the police, at the time of registration of the FIR, the reasons for their presence at the house of the deceased on the night of the occurrence. During cross-examination, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, stated: “It is correct that I did not mention the reason of my presence in the house of the victim on the night of occurrence in the FIR.” Likewise, Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) admitted during cross-examination that: “It is correct that I did not mention the reason of my presence in the house of the victim on the night of occurrence in the FIR.” Subsequently, during the investigation, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, sought to explain his presence at the place of occurrence by producing four wedding invitation cards of his maternal cousin, Tamkeen Akhtar (Exh-P-6 to P-9), along with her Nikah Nama (Exh-P-10). While appearing as a prosecution witness, he stated in his examination-in-chief that, during the investigation, he had handed over the said wedding invitation cards and Nikah Nama to the investigating officer, explaining that they had been present in Village Jand Sharif on the date of occurrence in connection with the rasm-e-Hina ceremony of his maternal cousin. However, during cross-examination, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, failed to disclose the name of the marriage hall where the wedding function had been held or the venue where the Walia took place. Had he attended the wedding ceremony of his maternal cousin at Jand Sharif, it would reasonably be expected that he would have been able to identify the venue of the functions. In this regard, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed as follows: “The marriage was of the daughter of Muhammad Ashfaq Akhtar, namely Tamqeen Akhtar. Barat arrived on 23.12.2019. I do not know the marriage hall in which function was held. I also do not know that in which marriage hall the Walima was held. I used to visit Jand Sharif because my maternal uncle lived there.” Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, further deposed that: “It is correct that there is no mentioning of Rasme Hina in my application Ex.PA and as such I have not mentioned in Exh.PA that I came in village Jand Sharif to attend that Rasme Hina.” Muhammad Mansha SI (PW-14), the investigating officer, deposed during the cross examination that: “I did not record the statement of bride and groom to confirm the marriage function for which invitation card was submitted to me. I did not record the statement of any person attending the function. I was not informed regarding any Rasmehina of Suleiman Atta s/o Atta r/o Jand Sharif. Nikah Nama dated 23.12.2019 of said Suleman was not produced before me.” Furthermore, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, admitted during cross- examination that the house situated opposite the house of the deceased was occupied by Waqas Ahmad (PW-2), son of Nazir Ahmed, who is also from their Baradari and a relative. Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, admitted during cross-examination that: “It is correct that none of the said persons is eye witness of the occurrence.” Both prosecution witnesses, i.e. namely Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), the alleged eyewitness, tried to establish their presence at the place of occurrence. In these circumstances, the presence of both witnesses at the place of occurrence does not stand satisfactorily established.

This Court also noted that Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) improved upon his statement to support the prosecution version. In these circumstances, I shall proceed directly to examine the material improvements and discrepancies in the prosecution evidence brought on record by the defence. During cross- examination, Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) admitted that: “I had made statement before police. It is correct that in my statement before police I mention about coming in the street on hearing the noise and did not mention about running. My statement was recorded once by police. It is correct that I mentioned about successive fires by accused Qamar Abbas in my statement before police. It is correct that I did not mention about fires hitting the car in my statement under section 161 Cr.PC. I had not recorded motive as land dispute in my statement under section 161 Cr.PC. I had not mentioned about sealing of parcel of blood stained cotton swabs and crime empties in my statement it is correct that I did not mention regarding the bulb installed with the shade of house of disease in my statement.” Both prosecution witnesses, i.e. namely Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), the alleged eyewitness, tried to establish their presence at the place of occurrence. In these circumstances, the presence of both witnesses at the place of occurrence does not stand satisfactorily established. More significantly, the inquest report (Exh.PH) does not bear any signatures of the witnesses nor it was mentioned names of the witnesses therein at the bottom on the last page. A perusal of the inquest report (Exh-PH) reveals that, in column No.4, the names and residences of the persons who identified the dead body were recorded as Waqas Ahmad (PW-2) and Qasim Munir (given up PW). The same names also appear on the last page of the inquest report (Exh-PH). Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), investigating officer, in his examination-in- chief stated that he was present at Golyana Chowk along with other police officials when Constable Nabeel Ashiq (not cited as PW) handed over to him a copy of the FIR and the complaint. Thereafter, he (PW-14) contacted the complainant (PW-11), who informed him that the dead body of Khushnood Akhtar (deceased) had been shifted to Civil Hospital, Kharian. The relevant portion of his testimony reads as follows: “After that I contacted with the complainant who told me that the body of deceased Khushnood Akhtar had been shifted to Civil Hospital Kharian.” Muhammad Munsha, SI (PW-14), investigating officer, further deposed that he proceeded to Civil Hospital, Kharian, along with the police officials, examined the dead body in the mortuary, prepared the injury statement (Exh-PY), inquest report (Exh-PH), and prepared the application for post-mortem examination (Exh-PG). Thereafter, he (PW-14) handed over the relevant documents and the dead body to Safdar Shahzad, Constable No. 3327/C (PW-7), for the purpose of conducting the post-mortem examination. Subsequently, he (PW-14) proceeded to the place of occurrence, where the complainant, the eyewitnesses and other respectable residents of the locality met him. Significantly, in his examination-in-chief, Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), did not depose that the complainant, the eyewitnesses or the residents accompanied him from the hospital to the place of occurrence. This omission assumes importance when considered alongside his testimony that he examined the dead body in the mortuary and prepared the relevant documents, including the inquest report (Exh-PH). A perusal of the inquest report (Exh-PH), however, raises further questions regarding the place where it was prepared. Although the investigating officer claimed to have prepared the report at Civil Hospital, Kharian, column No. 1 of the report mentions Mauza Jand Sharif, while column No. 24 refers to the dead body without specifying its location. Moreover, the place of preparation recorded on the last page of the report is “Gulyana”. These circumstances, when considered collectively with the discrepancies in the witnesses' accounts regarding the time of the police arrival, the unexplained circumstances surrounding the witnesses' presence at the place of occurrence, and the contents of the inquest report, cast serious doubt upon the prosecution's version regarding the presence of the alleged eyewitnesses at the relevant time. They also give rise to the doubt that the prosecution witnesses were planted. Waqas Ahmad (PW-2), a witness who identified the dead body, stated in examination-in-chief that: “On 23.12.2019, I alongwith Qasim Munir PW identified the dead body of deceased Khushnood Akhtar in THQ Hospital, Kharian at the time of post mortem examination , before the Medical Officer.” Waqas Ahmad (PW-2) deposed during cross-examination that: “I reached at hospital at 6:00 a.m. After my reaching at hospital post mortem was conducted within half an hour. Qasim Munir PW was also present with me. No other person and PWs were present there. Waqas Ahmad (PW-2) further deposed during cross-examination that: I.O did not obtain my signature on any document prior of autopsy. The aforesaid testimony of Waqas Ahmad (PW-2) casts doubt upon the authenticity and circumstances surrounding the preparation of the inquest report (Exh-PH). When this testimony is examined in conjunction with the contents of the inquest report (Exh-PH), further inconsistencies emerge. In column No. 3 of the report, Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), the investigating officer, recorded the date and time of the receiving information of the death as 23.12.2019 at 2:45 a.m. This entry is significant because the complainant, Majid Ali (PW-11), is stated to have reported the occurrence at the police station at 2:45 a.m. on the same date. The time of receiving information of the death raises questions regarding the chronology of events and the information available to the police at that stage. Furthermore, Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) stated that the police arrived at the place of occurrence at approximately 2:30 a.m./3:00 a.m. on 23.12.2019. Whereas Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed during cross-examination that he reached the place of occurrence at about 4:00 a.m. Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), the investigating officer, also stated during cross-examination that he reached the place of occurrence at about 4:00 a.m. The prosecution's account of the sequence in which the police received information, the FIR was registered, and the investigating officer proceeded to the hospital is, therefore, required to be scrutinized. According to one version emerging from the record, the relevant documents, including the application for registration of the case and a copy of the FIR, were forwarded through a police official, and Waqas Ahmad (PW-2) reached DHQ Hospital, Kharian, after receiving the information and the relevant documents. Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), however, deposed in his examination-in-chief that he was present at Gulyana Chowk, along with other police officials, when he received the information and obtained a copy of the FIR and the complaint from Constable Nabeel Ashiq (not cited as PW). He further stated that he thereafter proceeded to Civil Hospital, Kharian, where he examined the body of the deceased and prepared the relevant documents. The investigating officer’s account in his examination-in-chief regarding his whereabouts when he received the information differs materially from the account recorded by him in the inquest report (Exh-PH). Whereas in the column related to brief history of the case it is mentioned that: وے مقذمہ عىوان باال درج رجسٹر کر کےASI/DO "جس پر افتخار حسیه THQ تفتیش مقذمہ میرے عقب بھجوائی میں معہ ہمراہی مالزمان اطالع پا کر ہسپتال کھاریاں پہىچا ہوں وعش مقتول خوشىود اختر ڈیڈ ہاؤس "میں شماالجىوبا پڑی ہوئی ہے۔ This inconsistency, considered alongside the discrepancies concerning the signatures on the inquest report and the time at which the witnesses reached the hospital, casts serious doubt on the prosecution’s version of events and the veracity of its witnesses.

Furthermore, the delay between the time of death and the post- mortem examination assumes significance effect. The prosecution evidence indicates a delay of approximately eight (8) to fourteen (14) hours between the death and the post-mortem examination. According to the medical evidence, the post-mortem examination was conducted at 7:00 a.m on 23.12.2019. If the occurrence took place at 8:45 p.m. and Khushnood Akhtar (deceased) remained alive for approximately 30 minutes after sustaining the injuries, as suggested by the medical evidence, his time of death would be approximately 9:15 p.m. on 22.12.2019. Accordingly, the interval between his death and the post-mortem examination conducted at 7:00 a.m. on 23.12.2019 would be approximately 11 hours and 30 minutes. The Medical Officer stated that the interval between death and the post-mortem examination was between eight and fourteen hours which casts doubt upon the prosecution's time of occurrence. There are material contradictions between the ocular account and the medical evidence. Both prosecution witnesses, namely Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), the eyewitness, deposed that, when they came out of the house, they saw the appellant, Qamar Abbas, firing successive shots at Khushnood Akhtar (deceased) with his pump-action gun, which struck the latter on his legs. Thereafter, an unidentified person fired shots at the deceased with a 30-bore pistol, which also struck him on his legs, because of which Khushnood Akhtar sustained serious injuries and fell to the ground. The ocular account, therefore, suggests that the deceased was standing when he was fired upon by the appellant and his unidentified accomplice. However, the medical evidence presents a different picture. According to the medical record, the deceased sustained firearm injuries to the right lower limb/thigh near the knee, with four exit wounds, on right knee on its lateral aspect. Similarly, an entry wound was found on the left upper thigh, with a corresponding exit wound and blackening around the left knee. A perusal of diagram further indicates that the firearm injuries apparently directed from above to downwards. These wound characteristics that the deceased was not standing when the shots were fired at the deceased. If the deceased had been standing in the manner suggested by the ocular account, the nature and direction of the wounds would through and through. In the absence of such an explanation, the discrepancy between the ocular account and the medical evidence assumes significance. The medical evidence, when examined alongside the alleged eyewitnesses' account, casts doubt upon the prosecution's version of the manner in which the occurrence took place and, consequently, creates doubts on the presence of Majid Ali (PW-11) and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) at the place of occurrence. The scanned copy of the pictorial diagram (Exh-PF) is as under: This fact also creates doubt in the prosecution case as well as on the credibility and truthfulness of the statements of Majid Ali (PW-11) and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12). Therefore, I do not think it safe to rely on the evidence of these witnesses i.e. Majid Ali (PW-11) and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12). This also creates doubt about the genuineness of the version given by Majid Ali (PW-11) and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12). These aspects of the matter are sufficient to cast doubt about the authenticity of the F.I.R. This creates serious doubt about the genuineness of the prosecution story including presence of the complainant at the scene of occurrence. Delay in lodging the FIR often results in embellishment, which is a creature of an afterthought.

The motive set up by the prosecution in the written complaint (Exh.PA/1) and the F.I.R. (Exh.PA) and sought to be established through the testimony of Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12), remained unproved. The prosecution’s version in this regard was vague and hardly inspired confidence. During cross-examination, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed that: “However I do not know the title and name of the court where that litigation was pending. I do no know the area of land for which there was dispute. I did not produce any copy of litigation to the I.O. to prove the motive part.” Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) deposed during cross-examination that: - “There was no litigation between deceased and accused Qamar Abbas.” In these circumstances, I conclude that the alleged motive was an afterthought and remained unsubstantiated by any credible evidence.

The learned Deputy Prosecutor General (DPG) has emphasized that the vehicle of the deceased was recovered from the place of occurrence and that it had also sustained firearm hits. During cross-examination, Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, deposed that: “I have not mentioned on which side of the vehicle fire shots hit. No metal body of bullet was recovered from inside the vehicle.” Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) deposed during cross-examination that: - “It is correct that I did not mention about fires hitting the car in my statement u/s 161 Cr.P.C.” However, it is noteworthy that neither of the prosecution witnesses specified in their statements before the police or during their testimony before the Court, the side of the vehicle on which the firearm shots had struck.

As regards the recovery of 12 bore pump-action gun (Exh-P-2) from the residential house of the appellant, Qamar Abbas, and the positive report of the Punjab Forensic Science Agency (Exh-PBB), it is pertinent to observe that the prosecution has failed to establish the safe custody of the crime empties allegedly recovered from the place of occurrence. During cross-examination, Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) admitted that he had not mentioned in his statement recorded under Section 161, Cr.P.C., the sealing of the parcels containing blood-stained cotton swabs and crime empties. This omission creates doubt regarding the safe custody of the crime empties and, consequently, raises questions about the safe custody of the crime empties. Similarly, in columns Nos. 22 and 23 of the inquest report (Exh-PH) it is not mention of the recovery of crime empties from the place of occurrence. This omission further weakens the prosecution's claim regarding the recovery and subsequent handling of the crime empties and casts doubt upon the reliability of the positive report of the Punjab Forensic Science Agency (Exh- PBB).

As far as the recovery of the motorcycle (Exh-P-1) on 28.01.2020 from his in-laws’ house at the instance of the appellant, Qamar Abbas, is concerned, Fakhar Ijaz 1912/C (PW-4) admitted during cross-examination that: “We left the police station at 12.40 pm on official vehicle for recovery purpose in village Bijayran. We directly went to the said village without any stay in the way. I.O did not call any councilor, respectable and lumberdar of the locality. The neighborer of the recovery place was also not called by the I.O at the time of recovery. No inmate of the house was available and the house was bolted without lock. --- The place of recovery was residential house. I.O did not collect any information regarding the residents of said house. The recovered motorcycle was without number plate. --- All the doors of the rooms of the house were opened.” Muhammad Mansha, SI (PW-14), investigating officer deposed during cross- examination that: “In case diary dated 28.01.2020, I did not mention about visiting police station Kharian. It is correct that place of recovery of motorcycle from village Bijayran is in territorial jurisdiction of police station Saddar Kharian. It is correct that no one from the local public was joined in recovery proceedings.” It is also noteworthy that, according to the FIR, the accused persons fled from the place of occurrence on a motorcycle while resorting to firing. However, neither the FIR (Exh-PA) nor the relevant testimony of the prosecution witnesses provides any identifying particulars of the motorcycle allegedly used in the commission of the offence. In these circumstances, the recovery of motorcycle (P-1) from a house whose ownership or connection with the appellant was never established has no evidentiary value. The absence of any identifiable particulars linking the recovered motorcycle with the vehicle allegedly used by the assailants renders the recovery inconsequential to the prosecution's case. Consequently, the alleged recovery does not provide any reliable corroboration of the appellant's involvement in the occurrence.

Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case, the material available on the record, and the evidence adduced at trial, I am of the view that the prosecution has failed to present a true and reliable account of the occurrence. The prosecution version is beset with serious doubts, and the testimonies of Majid Ali (PW-11), the complainant, and Mudassar Iqbal (PW-12) do not inspire confidence. In view of these infirmities, and for the reasons enumerated hereinabove, I am persuaded to hold that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. Consequently, the conviction and sentence recorded by the trial Court cannot be sustained. In this regard, reliance is placed on Muhammad Akram v. The State (2009 SCMR 230), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan held that even a single circumstance creating reasonable doubt in a prudent mind as to the guilt of an accused entitles the accused to the benefit of that doubt, not as a matter of grace or concession, but as a matter of right.

Resultantly Criminal Appeal No.67154-J of 2022 is accepted. Conviction and sentence recorded by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 06.08.2022 is set aside as a consequence whereof, Qamar Abbas, appellant is ordered to be acquitted of the charge in case F.I.R. No. 244/2019, dated 23.12.2019, offence under Sections 302, 34 PPC, registered at Police Station, Gulyana, District Gujrat. The appellant Qamar Abbas is directed to be released forthwith, if not required in any other criminal case.

So far as Criminal Revision No. 67153 of 2022 filed by the complainant for enhancement of the sentence of the appellant/respondent No.1, Qamar Abbas, awarded by the trial court, is concerned, for the reasons aforesaid, the same is devoid of any legal force, which is accordingly dismissed.
